title: Option pricing models and put-call parity
body_md:
## Black-Scholes (European options)

Inputs: **spot, strike, time to expiry, volatility, risk-free rate, dividends**. Volatility is the only unobservable input, so the market quotes **implied volatility (IV)**, backed out from the premium.

## Binomial model

Builds a tree of up and down moves and values the option backwards; useful for American options.

## Put-call parity (European, no dividends)

**C − P = S − K × e^(−rt)** (or S − PV of K).

Example: S = 100, K = 100, PV of K = 97, P = 4: C = 4 + (100 − 97) = **7**.

If parity breaks, an arbitrage exists: buy the cheap side, sell the expensive side.

## Volatility types

| Type | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Historical** | Computed from past prices |
| **Implied** | Backed out of option prices |
| **India VIX** | Exchange index of expected near-term volatility |

> **Exam tip:** The one input to estimate in Black-Scholes is volatility.
example: VIX jumps from 12 to 20: options become more expensive across the board, as the market expects larger moves.
say: Implied volatility is what the market expects, not a prediction.
Put-call parity links calls, puts, spot and strike.
never: Parity never breaks, so no need to check.

check.why: Call minus put equals spot minus the present value of the strike.
